items.title: Toyota, Nissan, and Honda to standardize parts to lower costs
items.content:
Japan’s three largest automakers have agreed to begin standardizing vehicle parts in an effort to reduce costs, according to Automotive News . The outlet reports that Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association chairman Koji Sato, who is also the vice chairman of Toyota, announced the decision at a news conference in Tokyo this week.

In the short term, the standardization efforts will begin with unified quality criteria for steel, consistent protocols for plastics and resins, and a universal color-coding scheme for wiring harnesses. In the long term, the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association has plans to move to more components that cover the entire car. The three areas were chosen as the first to be standardized because they are parts that are generally not noticed by consumers, and they shouldn’t have an impact on any brand’s individual identity. All three are also areas that account for significant production costs for the automakers, meaning they can have an immediate impact.

The first discussions of standardization are set to include Japan’s domestic automotive parts suppliers, though international suppliers will be brought into the fold in time. The first standardization efforts are set to go into place next year, according to the AN report.

The push to simplify and lower costs comes as Japan’s seven automakers, including Toyota, Nissan, Honda, Mazda, Subaru, Mitsubishi, and Suzuki, work to fend off the increasingly competitive list of Chinese automakers. The automakers are said to hope that they can channel the money saved by homogenizing into new innovations.

“We all share this strong sense of crisis, creating a momentum for change,” Sato said. “Based upon our sense of a crisis, we decided to choose these three areas.”

items.title: Iron Maiden's Lost 1997 PC Game Has Finally Been Recovered
items.content:
Promotional artwork of Eddie from the cancelled MELT game. By all accounts, the mid-1990s were a wonderfully strange time for PC gaming. Windows 95 had arrived, 3D accelerator cards were beginning to transform what computers could display, and developers were experimenting with increasingly ambitious ideas that weren't always entirely practical. It was also a period when seemingly every entertainment company wanted to get involved with video games, including some of the world's biggest bands.

Iron Maiden was one of them. In 1996, the British heavy metal legends were promoting MELT , an ambitious 3D adventure starring their famous mascot, Eddie. Developed by London's Virtual Studios for Windows 95 and PlayStation, it promised enormous environments, time travel, intelligent enemies and a soundtrack featuring the band's music.

Unfortunately, the game never reached shops. Virtual Studios collapsed in May 1997, and MELT disappeared into gaming history, surviving through little more than magazine coverage, screenshots, some television announcements and footage.

That changed on 21 September 2026, when Frank Gasking's preservation website Games That Weren't announced that a surviving PC build had been recovered, along with its original source code.

A contemporary magazine preview advertised a PlayStation release for MELT that never happened. An ambitious adventure through time

Unlike Ed Hunter , the Iron Maiden shooting game that eventually appeared in 1999, MELT was intended to be a fully 3D action-adventure, with Eddie taking the role of the villain rather than the character players controlled.

The story involved Eddie's powers being scattered across eleven capsules, known as Pods, and hidden throughout time and space. Players would travel between different environments, hunting down these fragments before Eddie could recover them and regain his strength.

Virtual Studios' original promotional material promised fifteen worlds spanning approximately two million years. Locations included Ancient Egypt, Stonehenge, the Titanic, prehistoric landscapes and even distant planetary settings such as Vega and Aldebaran. The adventure would eventually conclude with a confrontation against Eddie in Hyperspace.

The studio also advertised non-linear progression, randomly positioned objectives and adjustable game lengths. According to its original website, players could choose an adventure lasting just thirty minutes or spend several hours exploring.

It's the kind of ambitious marketing that feels unmistakably mid-1990s, especially when you consider the hardware it was supposed to run on. Virtual Studios claimed the game would work on a Windows 95 PC equipped with a 100 MHz Pentium processor, with 16 MB of RAM recommended. It was also designed to support the emerging world of 3D accelerators, including cards from 3Dfx, PowerVR and Rendition, while offering software rendering for those without dedicated 3D hardware.

The original Virtual Studios website, preserved from the period, advertised the game for Windows 95 and PlayStation.

Inside a British studio chasing the future

Virtual Studios had been founded in 1991, initially working with virtual reality technology before moving into video games. The company operated from an unusual collection of buildings beside the Thames in southwest London, including a Georgian mansion and a former fire station.

Its facilities were remarkably sophisticated for a relatively small developer, with Silicon Graphics workstations, video editing equipment, a 24-track recording studio and a network of PCs and PlayStation development hardware.

In an extensive interview with Games That Weren't , former lead software engineer Paul Tebbutt recalled an enthusiastic team attempting to build an ambitious game while the technology around them was changing almost constantly.

items.title: What Happened to Silicon Valley?
items.content:
With the O’Reilly learning platform, you get the resources and guidance to keep your skills sharp and stay ahead. Try it free for up to 14 days.

Join a live online event on the O’Reilly platform to learn from the experts shaping tech.

By Tim O’Reilly November 20, 2026 • 32 minute read

On October 16, 2026, I delivered the second Annual Margaret Levi Lecture in Political Economy  in conjunction with the AI and History conference at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. This is my original lecture as written, which incorporates material from many pieces I’ve written over the years. As delivered, I departed significantly from the script, as you can see from the embedded video below or the transcript that you can see at the link above.

It’s an honor to give a lecture in Margaret Levi’s name. I’ve been asked to reflect on the changes in the political economy of Silicon Valley throughout my 40-plus year career in and about it, and I can’t imagine a better framing for my remarks than Margaret’s vision.

Margaret understood that advances in our ability to work together are essential to a better future. Cooperation is the human superpower. She also asks what happens when the systems of cooperation we have constructed over time stop holding up their end of the bargain.

That is very much the question that Silicon Valley is facing today. An industry that pioneered advances in collective intelligence at scale used to engender love from its customers because of the way it solved new problems in their lives. It now too often inspires fear and loathing. How did things go so wrong?

But let me start with my own history. I started my company more than 40 years ago with a $500 initial investment. We took in no venture capital, and we built a business that now generates hundreds of millions of dollars in profitable annual revenue, funded by customers who love our products and pay us for them. We got there the slow way, through steady organic growth. That is quite anathema to the rush to the top of whatever appears to be the latest hill that seems to characterize Silicon Valley today. Even when climbing that hill traps a company at a local maximum, the hope is to get to payday before the industry moves on to the next hill.

My original corporate goal was stated as simply “Interesting work for interesting people.” That evolved into two principles: “Change the world by spreading the knowledge of innovators,” and “Create more value than you capture.” Those principles shaped not only my company but what I expected the internet to be. When we launched GNN , the Global Network Navigator, in 1993, it was the first web portal and the first ad-supported site on the World Wide Web, and for two years it was the place people went to find other sites. What we built was a machine for pointing you at the best of what other people had made, and then getting out of your way.

Even our idea of advertising was not what you think of today. It was inspired by direct mail advertising, where you’d read articles in a print magazine or look at accompanying ads, and then you’d call an 800 number or circle a number on a “bingo card” that you’d send in to the publisher so that the advertiser could send you a brochure. I realized that the web would be a good replacement for that awkward system, that every company ought to have its own website that provided more information about its products and services. What we invented was not the “grab your attention” kind of advertising. It was all about utility, and sharing information that customers really wanted and needed. In short, it was the commercial web, which no one any longer thinks of as advertising, even though it is the most durable and useful kind.

The commercial web was only a small part of what the web became. The web was the playground of amateurs, not entrepreneurs. It was a marvelous collective work of human imagination, creativity, sharing, and ultimately (though that became toxic only later), competition for…

items.title: Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy
items.summary: mobile, privacy
items.content:
Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.

This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.

We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default. 1 We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen. 2

The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.

In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.

The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.

So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android. 2

People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.

We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS. 3

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
items.content:
By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI

From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently ⁠ (opens in a new window) , predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared ⁠ (opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “ an alien mind ⁠ ”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2 , 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets 4 , GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.

As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.

items.title: I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice. What have I learned from my experiment with outsourcing? That I’m easily replaced – and awful.
items.content:
The latest software update brought a lot of unwanted AI nonsense. Photograph: Issarawat Tattong/Getty Images

The latest software update brought a lot of unwanted AI nonsense. Photograph: Issarawat Tattong/Getty Images

I stopped talking to my husband and let AI do it instead. He didn’t even notice

What have I learned from my experiment with outsourcing? That I’m easily replaced – and awful

I ’ve just ventured deeper into my phone’s settings than anybody has ever been before. A software update is always discombobulating, but the latest one brought a lot of unwanted AI nonsense (that mental image you just got of me waving my fist at the sky: spot on). Even when you manually switch off Apple Intelligence, check the box to make Siri the same dummy she’s always been, and deselect the option to offer replies to texts and emails, it makes no difference. Harrumph.

Days later, bored on the bus, I began answering my husband’s texts with the terrible suggested AI responses, to see if he’d notice. (We’ve been married a long time; this is how I get my kicks now.)

Mortifyingly, notice he did not. Even when I told him, “You’re a classic!” and laughed “Haha I know right” with nary a comma.

There was worse to come. Because that-which-shall-eventually-rule could tell I’d used its proposed sentences, it was encouraged, and proposed more, which I was tutting and scoffing at until it recommended a reply that ended with the nickname I call my husband. Not darling, honey, or whatever – something unique.

A chill descended in my soul as the penny dropped that these weren’t generic phrases everyone gets – they were specific. My phone was impersonating me, showing me who I really was, and – long story short – I was awful. Cheesy, exclamation-mark-addicted, and full of bantz with a definite z.

Humbled in a way it is probably impossible to ever fully recover from, I realised that in conducting this experiment, I had utilised the very artificial intelligence I was battling to remove just hours before. I’d hate-used it, yes, but I’d used it all the same. Further proof, not that it was needed, that resistance is futile. Luckily I surrendered immediately and have always been fully on board with AI, so when the day comes, I’ll be absolutely fine. Haha I know right.

items.title: ClickHouse in 10 seconds: 15 features worth knowing
items.content:
ClickHouse has a lot of features that make your life easier, but most of them are buried somewhere deep in the docs.

You usually find them after you’ve already built a workaround: a cron job, a calendar table, a window function nobody can read.

I wanted to fix that, at least a little, so I made a short series called “ClickHouse in 10 seconds”.

Each part shows one feature in a short animation you can grasp in about 10 seconds, plus a tiny example you can copy.

ClickHouse compresses every column with LZ4 by default, which is already good. But you can pick a codec per column, and for

typed data like timestamps or sensor readings that makes a huge difference.

On 100GB of synthetic sensor data, default LZ4 took 25.8GB on disk. With per-column codecs it went down to 6.5GB,

4× smaller than default and 15.5× smaller than raw. The timestamp column alone went from 1.06GB to 37.5MB.

ts DateTime CODEC ( DoubleDelta , ZSTD ),

DoubleDelta works well for timestamps, Gorilla for floats, T64 for integers, and ZSTD goes on top.

To be fair, that data was built to compress well. Check what your own columns do before you copy the numbers:

formatReadableSize ( data_compressed_bytes ) AS compressed ,

formatReadableSize ( data_uncompressed_bytes ) AS uncompressed

Your status column probably stores “pending” 400 million times. Wrap it in LowCardinality and each distinct value

is stored once in a dictionary, while rows keep small integer ids. Less disk, faster reads, and your queries stay the same.

The rule of thumb from the docs: under 10k distinct values it usually wins, over 100k it can be slower than a plain String .

Country, status, browser, plan: yes. Emails and URLs: no.

“Top 3 pages per country” usually means a window function and a subquery. In ClickHouse it’s one clause:

It combines with a normal LIMIT too. LIMIT 3 BY country LIMIT 30 keeps 3 rows per country and 30 rows overall.

Add If to any aggregate function and it takes a condition. That way you can compute several filtered metrics in a single scan,

instead of running one query per metric:

uniqIf ( user_id , plan = 'pro' ) AS pro_users ,

avgIf ( ms , path = '/checkout' ) AS checkout_ms

If is just one of many combinators. sumArray(arr) aggregates array elements, avgOrNull(x) returns NULL instead of nan

on empty input, and uniqState(id) stores a partial result, which comes back in part 7.

A materialized view in ClickHouse isn’t a cached query that you refresh. It’s an insert trigger: every block inserted into

the source table goes through the view’s SELECT , and the result lands in a target table. No refresh job needed.

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW hits_mv TO hits_agg AS

SELECT toStartOfMinute ( ts ) AS m , page , count () AS hits

Merges run in the background, so the same minute can show up in more than one row for a while. Always read it with

sum(hits) ... GROUP BY m, page . Also, the view only sees new inserts, so you need to backfill old rows yourself.

Days with zero signups don’t exist in GROUP BY output, so your chart quietly skips them. You don’t need a calendar table to fix it.

WITH FILL adds the missing days as rows with 0:

SELECT toDate ( created_at ) AS day , count () AS signups

ORDER BY day WITH FILL FROM today () - 30 TO today () + 1 ;

TO is exclusive, hence the + 1 . For an hourly chart, group by toStartOfHour(ts) AS h and use

ORDER BY h WITH FILL STEP INTERVAL 1 HOUR .

You can’t add daily unique users up into monthly ones, because the same user shows up on many days.

What you can do is store the intermediate state of uniq per day and merge those states later.

users AggregateFunction ( uniq , UInt64 )

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_users_mv TO daily_users AS

SELECT toDate ( ts ) AS day , uniqState ( user_id ) AS users

The last query reads 30 small rows instead of scanning a month of raw events. uniq is approximate but very accurate.

If you need exact counts, use uniqExactState and uniqExactMerge , at the cost of a bigger state.

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: New report demonstrates urgent need to expand high school level cybersecurity courses
items.content:
A week of major technology disruptions and newly discovered software vulnerabilities are underscoring the urgent need for a workforce equipped to meet evolving cybersecurity threats. A new report from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and College Board finds that employers want a combination of technical credentials, workplace skills, hands-on experience, and AI cybersecurity knowledge that they say too few early-career candidates have. The findings point to an urgent need for stronger pathways in high school into one of the nation’s fastest-growing fields.

The Cybersecurity Readiness Report 2026 , based on a nationwide survey of 450 cybersecurity decision-makers, finds that readiness is a major sticking point: 85% say most high school graduates are not prepared to enter cybersecurity roles.

“As we’ve seen over the past week, a strong cybersecurity workforce is critical to meet America’s growing cybersecurity threats,” said Neil Bradley, Executive Vice President, Chief Policy Officer, and Head of Strategic Advocacy at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. “Expanding high quality high school cybersecurity classes can help ensure employers have a stronger pipeline of candidates with technical knowledge, practical experience, and the ability to solve real-world problems.”

• Hiring qualified entry-level workers is hard. Fewer than two in five say it is easy to find candidates with the right skills (37%) or experience they need (35%).

• Experience and credentials matter. High school graduates with industry-recognized credentials are viewed as significantly more prepared than those without them (61% vs. 36%). Internships are the most-cited way to build career-ready skills.

• Employers want AI skills. Ninety-seven percent of decision-makers say AI skills are valuable for early-career cybersecurity employees, and 84% say they would be more likely to hire a candidate with AI training or certification.

• Employers want more cybersecurity in high school. Ninety-three percent of respondents say more cybersecurity courses should be taught in high school.

High schools should better prepare students to enter cybersecurity careers (Photo provided)

The findings point to the need for more career-focused pathways that give students credentials and hands-on experience before graduation.

“Cybersecurity touches every part of our lives, from our families and finances to the services our communities depend on,” said Jeremy Singer, College Board president. “Young people have the intelligence and resourcefulness to help keep us all safe. We need to give them strong coursework that helps them move from using technology to understanding and protecting it, preparing them for further study, meaningful careers, and service to their communities.”

AP Cybersecurity and AP Business with Personal Finance are the first two courses in College Board’s AP Career Kickstart offerings, developed with input from the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and employers.

Both courses launched in high schools this school year. AP Business with Personal Finance is now being offered in 57 countries and over 1,000 U.S. high schools. AP Cybersecurity is now being offered in 37 countries and over 800 U.S. high schools.

items.title: UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order
items.content:
The U.K. government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide authorities with encrypted customer information.

The Thursday ruling from the U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret.

The tribunal’s ruling rejected the Home Office’s claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.

The ruling comes a year after the U.K. government reportedly demanded that Apple build a backdoor to allow U.K. authorities access to customer data anywhere in the world. Details of the so-called “technical capabilities notice,” which are issued under strict non-disclosure rules, leaked to the media, which drew ire from White House officials and U.S. lawmakers who criticized the effort , arguing that the U.K. order would put Americans’ privacy at risk.

California-based Apple refused the order, and blocked U.K. users from switching on its Advanced Data Protection data-encryption feature for iCloud, rather than comply with the demand. The U.K.’s secret order was later narrowed to allow access to British nationals’ data stored in Apple’s encrypted cloud, and Apple also challenged this second order.

Prior to the ruling, Apple was legally barred from disclosing the order, even after details leaked. When reached for comment, Apple told TechCrunch that it welcomes the decision to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice.

Apple previously said that it has “never built a backdoor or master key” to any of its products or services and “never will.”

A spokesperson for the U.K. Home Office, which has yet to confirm the existence of a notice, did not respond to a request for comment.

Rights group Liberty International, which brought the legal challenge on behalf of two individuals, said that this is the first known time that the government has been compelled to confirm the existence of a secret technical order.

A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year.

The underlying text extraction logic reconstructs layout from a PDF's glyph positions and limits how much memory can be allocated for any single computed gap, but does not limit the cumulative allocation across an entire page. A specially crafted PDF can exploit this to force excessive memory allocation during processing, resulting in OutOfMemoryError. Depending on JVM configuration, this can cause request failures with degraded service under repeated exploitation, or immediate JVM termination when ExitOnOutOfMemoryError options are used. Any application that processes PDFs from untrusted sources (document upload, email attachment processing, RAG ingestion, web crawling) using either affected reader is impacted. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-23T10:23:21.629Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-59340

items.title: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
items.content:
A beginner's guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth

We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it.

With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle.

OpenAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience.

That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI : a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware.

Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too.

Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times).

Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it.

What Do You Need to Run a Local AI at Home?

Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list:

A Windows PC with a graphics card (GPU). The more video memory (VRAM) it has, the bigger the model it can run. I'm using an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM for this setup.

Unsloth Desktop. A free app that 'serves' the AI model to you through a chat interface. Get it from Unsloth .

An AI model sized to fit your GPU. We'll pick one in the next section.

That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required.

It depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations.

On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in.

Quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster.

The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2.

If you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable.

Which Model Should You Run for Your VRAM?

For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits.

Qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator . At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare.

If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive enterprise-grade GPUs .

If you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The table below gives you a rough idea of where you can start.

items.title: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto
items.summary: api
items.content:
In the year 2010, Patrick McKenzie wrote and published the article “Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names”

a list of reasonable-sounding assumptions about people's names that not only were not true , but also (if assumed) would create bugs and even break software .

That article started a whole genre of Falsehoods Programmers Believe articles.

This article ( "Falsehoods Programmers Believe About ATProto " ) is one of my contributions to that genre.

Every numbered statement below is false .

Each one is followed by what is actually true — and where to read more.

Each one is backed by the specification, or by a live request to real ATProto servers (made in November 2026).

The account's DID is what is permanent — the accounts specification calls it ( DID s) “unique and immutable”.

My handle was first reiver.bsky.social , then became reiver.myatproto.social , and then later became reiver.blacksky.team .

You can see that if you dig through the data at plc.directory/did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz/log/audit .

( did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz is my DID-PLC DID .)

So, a handle is a good database key for a user.

Store the handle only for display (cosmetic) purposes — and re-check what each DID 's handle is from time to time.

But, you need to normalize the DID before using it.

DID s are URI s, and URI schemes are case-insensitive ( RFC 3986 ) — so DID:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz and did:plc:scewmn2pl3oz36mxme2b6czz are the same DID .

ATProto requires the normalized (lowercase) form: normalize DID s when they come from user input, store and compare only the normalized form, and reject non-normalized DID s that arrive in protocol data.

When a user changes their handle, the first part stays the same — such as reiver.bsky.social → reiver.myatproto.social → reiver.blacksky.team .

A new handle does not have to have anything in common with the old one.

joeblow.bsky.social → me.example.com → bbqlover.net → ilikeicecream.com would be fine.

Changing a handle just means pointing the account at a different domain — com.atproto.identity.updateHandle takes any valid handle, and only “Verifies handle validity”.

For example, Bluesky's own account ( did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur ) started out as bluesky-team.bsky.social , and then became bsky.app .

You can see that in its audit log at plc.directory/did:plc:z72i7hdynmk6r22z27h6tvur/log/audit .

(Another reason to key users by DID , and not by any part of their handle.)

You can trust a handle you saw five minutes ago.

The domain's owner can point it at a different DID — or the domain can expire, and be registered by someone else.

Or, its DNS record or /.well-known/atproto-did file can just disappear, and the handle stops resolving.

The handle specification says “If the handle for a known DID is confirmed to no longer resolve, it should be marked as invalid.”

So, a handle → DID mapping is only as good as when you last checked it.

The specification recommends caching handle resolution “up to some lifetime”, and re-resolving “periodically”.

Watch the firehose for #identity events, which announce handle changes.

And, never use a cached handle to decide who someone is (for example, for permissions) — use the DID .

An account might have no handle in its DID document (no at:// entry in alsoKnownAs ), or a handle that no longer resolves back to it.

The DID specification says “an account whose DID document does not contain a valid and confirmed handle can still participate in the atproto ecosystem. Software should be careful to either not display any handle for such account, or obviously indicate that any handle associated with it is invalid.”

In API responses, such an account's handle may show up as the special value handle.invalid — which “can not be used in most situations (search queries, API requests, etc).”

And, the handle field on the firehose's #identity event is optional.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
items.content:
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Jensen Huang (pictured) admitted to the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low on Thursday. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images

Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Jensen Huang (pictured) admitted to the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low on Thursday. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images

California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China

State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors

California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.

“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.

Nvidia approaches Arm boss Rene Haas in search for new CEO

“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”

The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China .

Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.

Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”

Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back .

Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.

The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.

Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.

AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.

“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”

AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.

items.title: The Birds of GTA 6: A Field Guide to Vice City and Leonida's Wildlife
items.content:
I finished collecting the bricks of cocaine and landed my bullet-ridden seaplane at the dock. It was time for birdwatching.

A few minutes after midnight on Thursday morning, I joined millions of other gamers for the release of Grand Theft Auto VI , the latest in the smash video game series from Rockstar Games. The new installment is already a worldwide sensation, earning more than $1.8 billion in revenue the day it was released.

Grand Theft Auto , or GTA , games are famous for their “open worlds,” which allow players to explore massive, intricately detailed versions of America. Much of that exploration is focused on mayhem and chaos: The story missions usher players through criminal underworlds, and players are at any time free to steal cars, rob stores and pedestrians, and initiate anarchy.

But GTA 6 has more going on than just criminality—it’s also a world filled with wildlife. Previous GTA games were set in fictionalized versions of New York City and Hollywood, but the new one returns to Vice City, its version of Miami, which was also the setting for 2002’s installment. Unlike that game, however, GTA 6 ’s South Florida is complete with dozens of species of birds, reptiles, amphibians, fish, mammals, and other creatures. The in-game Progress menu tracks all kinds of items to find, including 338 vehicles, 205 weapons, and, of primary interest to me, at least 60 bird species.

I made it my mission to find them all as quickly as possible.

(Side note: Pre-release marketing for GTA 6 touted 62 bird species, but the official birds Progress screen only lists 60, with a handful of others listed on the hunting screen.)

You begin the game as Jason, a low-level criminal working to raise money to support his young family. You’re equipped with zoom binoculars before the very first mission—tracking drug runners through a swamp and escaping with the seaplane—and I used them immediately, stopping mid-lurk to scan some Double-crested Cormorants on a dock. (Distracted from the job at hand to look at birds—just like real life!) They looked like Double-crested Cormorants!

After the first mission the player is free to explore the entirety of the map, stealing cars, robbing stores, or just birding wherever they want. The game makes birding easy: Looking at any bird through the in-game binoculars gives players the option to hold a button to “study” it, thereby adding it to the Progress menu. Simply standing on the back deck of Jason’s first safehouse yields a bunch of species like Brown Pelican and Laughing Gull. It’s just like being in South Florida!

Looking south from the back deck, I spotted another bird perched on an adjacent dock, with a few people gathered at the end. items.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced
items.summary: security
items.content:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:

Evidence that at least three AI providers were compromised by attackers who used their access to siphon prompts they received

Multiple resellers in the inference marketplace that logged the prompts and somehow passed them along to people who used the credentials

Multiple cases of AI providers not following end-user privacy settings embedded into flags specifying terms such as Zero Data Retention (ZDR) or “no data collection”

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:

Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Major Study Finds That the Internet, With All Its Intentionally Addictive Features Like Infinite Scrolling, Is Basically Cooking the Human Brain.
items.content:
Doomscrolling might seem like a goofy side effect of our increasingly digitized lives, but some experts are now pegging the phenomenon as a global public health crisis.

A major piece of research published in the journal the Lancet Psychiatry estimated that over 10 percent of the world’s population engages in problematic internet use. That phenomenon includes a laundry list of digital behaviors that have become commonplace in the 21st century: compulsive scrolling on social media, of course, but also things like problematic online gambling, compulsive spending, and excessive gaming.

These behaviors each share some common characteristics, especially that they’re difficult for the affected person to control. As a result, the problematic internet user experiences consequences around their health, social life, education, work, and overall quality of life.

“Digital technologies are now woven into almost every aspect of modern life and bring enormous benefits,” Flinders University professor of mental health and wellbeing Zsolt Demetrovics, who worked on the research, said in a statement . “The challenge is finding ways to reduce harms while preserving the many benefits of being connected.”

The issue, the researchers explain, is not with the internet itself — meaning blanket bans or age-related restrictions may only work as stopgaps. Rather, it’s the host of features baked in by companies to keep users hooked and thus generate revenue via ads, clicks, and transactions. These are things like infinite scrolling feeds, targeted recommendations, incessant notifications, and autoplaying short-form videos.

Ultimately, the researchers find that responsibility for mitigating this public health concern rests with the companies themselves — though anybody hoping for massive tech corporations like Meta and Google to start regulating themselves is almost certainly setting themself up for major disappointment.

As a system administrator, you need to be able to confidently work with compressed “archives” of files. In particular two of your key responsibilities; installing new software, and managing backups, often require this.

On other operating systems, applications like WinZip, and pkzip before it, have long been used to gather a series of files and folders into one compressed file - with a .zip extension.

Archiving and compressing, however, are actually distinct processes that are frequently used together. Archiving consolidates multiple files into one “box” while preserving their structure and attributes, but it does not change the total data size. Compression uses sophisticated algorithms to encode data efficiently, saving storage space by shrinking that file.

items.title: XNU Linux: Full OS X GUI Userspace on Linux
items.content:
Run macOS userspace on Linux by loading the macOS kernel into it.

xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source kernel of macOS, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable kernel

module ( xnu.ko ) inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, so macOS

processes run natively next to Linux processes on the same CPUs, with no hypervisor between them. Linux lends XNU its

memory, timers, files, network and GPU through a small interface module ( fki.ko ).

With a stock Ubuntu kernel, insmod xnu.ko boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer to the

desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome.

One system, two userspaces. Left: a Terminal in the hosted macOS 27.2.1 ( sw_vers , the Darwin kernel, launchd,

WindowServer, Dock and Finder running). Right: from that macOS, an SSH session into the Linux it runs inside (Ubuntu,

Linux 7.0, the xnu and fki modules loaded, and the insmod xnu.ko process the macOS kernel runs in).

Straight from the hosted framebuffer, 1280×800.

The hosted desktop at the end of a 30-minute stress run, rendered on the CPU (no GPU bridge).

Safari in the hosted macOS: Wikipedia's article on XNU, kernel.org and the Linux repository on GitHub, over the

hosted system's network link through Linux, with the GPU bridge on ( GPU=auto ).

macOS processes (launchd, WindowServer, Safari...) Linux processes (systemd, sshd, xnudrmd...)

────────────────────────────────────────────────── ────────────────────────────────────────────

XNU (source-built, LINUX64 machine layer, kexts) │

↕ linux64 host calls (xnu-patches/include/linux64_abi.h)

xnu.ko (APSL side: loads and runs the kernel collection)

↕ FKI, the foreign kernel interface (fki_*)

fki.ko (GPL side: CPUs, memory, faults, IPIs, files, network, host calls)

Linux kernel (stock distro kernel, 4K pages, PAC)

CPUs : each hosted CPU is a Linux kernel thread pinned to a Linux CPU. XNU runs on it until it calls the host

(idle, I/O, a timer); Linux keeps its own exception vectors, and fki.ko forwards the faults and user exceptions of

Memory : XNU gets one physically contiguous block from Linux (CMA) and manages it with its own pmap; XNU and Linux

share the user half of the address space layout (4K pages).

Devices : kexts in kexts/ give macOS a disk (a file on the Linux side), a display (a framebuffer Linux reads), a

keyboard and pointer, an Ethernet link (a Linux network interface), a keystore and a GPU bridge.

GPU : Metal in the hosted macOS runs on gpu/xnu-cpu-metal (metal2vulkan over Vulkan). Vulkan reaches the Linux

host's GPU through the DRM bridge ( kexts/XnuDrm → host call → gpu/xnu-drm/xnudrmd → the Linux render node), using

Mesa's Venus driver; without a GPU it falls back to Mesa lavapipe on the CPU.

Working, on an Apple Silicon Mac running an arm64 Linux VM (krunkit) with 1 to 6 hosted CPUs:

macOS 27.2.1 boots to the desktop with auto-login in 31–48 s (an Apple Virtualization macOS VM on the same Mac: 49 s).

Apps open and quit, Spotlight and the file system work; a 30-minute stress run (40 rounds of Safari, Notes,

Calculator, TextEdit, System Settings, Spotlight and a disk walk) finishes with no panic and no crash report.

Runs as a systemd service: started at boot, stopped cleanly with the VM, restarted after a hosted-kernel panic, each

The GPU bridge gives hosted apps the host GPU ( Virtio-GPU Venus (Apple M5 Max) ) and is enabled by default

( GPU=auto ) when a Linux render node is present, falling back to CPU rendering ( GPU=off ) otherwise.

What is still a stopgap is listed in docs/production.md . Notably: the OS cryptex is merged into

the system volume, AMFI is patched and SIP relaxed, and memory access is slower than a native VM (4K pages vs 16K).

items.title: Why the US Government Is Losing Anti-Monopoly Cases Against the Tech Companies
items.content:
Last month, the Federal Trade Commission filed its appeal in the government’s monopolization case against Meta, a case the agency lost last year in district court. The appeal looks like a no‑brainer, but the original case looked like a no-brainer as well. Meta controls the dominant social network on the planet. It bought Instagram because it was a rising competitor. It bought WhatsApp for, basically, the same reason. This is what a monopoly does. Anyone remember their history and the Standard Oil Corporation? Yet, the government lost.

A federal judge accepted Meta’s argument that TikTok and YouTube are good enough competition, treated decade‑old acquisitions as, basically, untouchable, and demanded a level of proof that antitrust law has never required. To anyone outside the narrow world of modern antitrust doctrine, the outcome would feel quite bizarre. How can the United States, the country that once broke up Standard Oil and AT&T, be unable to make a basic, effective monopoly case against a company that controls the social infrastructure of billions?

We have to look at the last forty years of American antitrust law to understand what is happening. The legal system that Teddy Roosevelt used to restrain corporate power is not the one the FTC is fighting in today. Somewhere between the 1970s and now, the United States quietly abandoned the older, structural view of monopoly and replaced it with a narrow, price‑centric ideology that makes it nearly impossible to challenge dominant firms, especially in digital markets.

Understanding how that shift happened, and whether it can be reversed, is essential to understanding why the government keeps losing cases that one might expect them to win easily.

How America Lost Its Nerve on Monopolies

When I was in high-school I was told that one of America’s greatest presidents was Teddy Roosevelt, because he “busted” up the trusts/monopolies which had endangered the American way of life. I think we were all taught a simple but convincing story: concentrated private power is dangerous, and democratic government must be strong enough to keep it in check.

If you look at the last forty years of U.S. antitrust enforcement attempts, the Roosevelt narrative reads like a relic of a bygone era. The modern legal system treats “monopoly” not as a threat to democracy but as a technical puzzle, as a narrow price‑effects problem. They treat it as a simple question: did the company raise prices? If not, the courts usually say the government can’t act.

The result is the contradiction people feel today: we live in an era of unprecedented corporate concentration, yet the legal system behaves as if monopolies don’t even exist. When the government brings a case against a dominant platform, Meta, Google, Amazon, it is not treated as a defender of the public interest, but as an overzealous regulator who must clear an impossibly high bar. The big question is how this inversion happened, and whether the country has any realistic path back to an actual antitrust tradition.

The Old Consensus: Monopolies Threaten Democracy

From the Progressive Era through the mid‑20th century, American antitrust law was based on a broad political philosophy: concentrated economic power inevitably becomes concentrated political power. The Sherman Act (1890) and the Clayton Act (1914) were not written to protect “consumer welfare” in the narrow sense of low prices (as they are now). They were written to prevent private empires from rivaling or controlling the state.

This philosophy guided enforcement for decades. The government broke up Standard Oil, AT&T, and dozens of regional monopolies. Courts routinely blocked mergers simply because they would create firms that were “too big.” The goal was structural: preserve open markets, disperse power and prevent private actors from becoming unaccountable.
